summary:
AgriFusion BD is a Bangladesh-first crop-rotation decision-support platform. A farmer draws a field on a satellite map, and the app combines NASA POWER weather data (rain and temperature) with NASA HLS satellite greenness and soil information to suggest three rotation choices, each with plain reasons, in Bangla and English. Agricultural officers can review cases and send a rover to check the field on the ground.

It answers the Field Shift challenge by comparing rotations — including the one the farmer already grows — and showing the evidence, benefits, gaps, and risks behind each option, so the farmer makes the final call, not the app.And the best crop rotation choices are ready with real evidence. 

It matters because Bangladeshi farming is under strain: floods, drought, and salinity are degrading soils, and about one million farming families need emergency agricultural assistance (FAO, 2026). With most farms small and fragmented, one wrong rotation can cost a family its season. AgriFusion BD turns open NASA data into advice a farmer can actually use — starting in Rajshahi, then across Bangladesh, then worldwide.
details:
What it does and how it works

AgriFusion BD is a crop-rotation decision-support platform for Bangladeshi farmers. A farmer draws their field on a satellite map. The app combines NASA POWER weather data (rainfall and temperature) with NASA HLS satellite greenness and soil information, then suggests three crop-rotation choices — including the one the farmer already grows — each with plain reasons, in Bangla and English. An agricultural officer sees the same data, reviews farmer cases, and assigns field checks to a small rover, which measures soil nutrients, water, and heat on the ground. The farmer makes the final decision; the app supports their judgment, it never replaces it. A working demo is live at https://rakatashraf.github.io/AgriFusionBD/

Benefits

It turns free, open NASA data into advice a farmer can actually use, in their own language, without expensive equipment. Because it compares rotations side by side — with the evidence, benefits, gaps, and risks for each — a farmer can see why a rotation is suggested, not just what to plant. The officer-and-rover loop adds ground truth to satellite data, and the soil-health focus means rotations are chosen to strengthen the soil over seasons, not just chase one harvest.

Intended impact

We start in Rajshahi, then scale across Bangladesh and worldwide. The need is urgent: about one million farming families need emergency agricultural assistance (FAO, 2026), 99% of farms are small and fragmented, saline land is spreading, and Rajshahi's groundwater has fallen nearly 4 metres since 1990. If rotations improve, soils get stronger, farms survive floods and dry spells better, and families keep more of each season. This is a working demo and a validation plan — the next step is testing it against real fields in Rajshahi across a full growing season before claiming results.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software

The working demo is a TypeScript web app with an interactive satellite map (MapLibre, Esri World Imagery), hosted on GitHub Pages. The backend design is Django with PostGIS for field and case data. Satellite-data and crop-modelling work is in Python, using NASA POWER and HLS, with SMAP, SoilGrids, WorldCover, and Copernicus DEM in the modelling workstream. The field rover is the AgriRover-Q design — a small quadruped built around a Raspberry Pi 4B — developed as a low-cost handheld Community Scout Kit rather than a large machine.

How it is creative

Most farm apps hand down a single answer. AgriFusion BD does the opposite: it shows three options with reasons and lets the farmer choose. It pairs the sky (satellites) with the ground (a small rover and a local officer) — two kinds of evidence, not one. And it is designed Bangla-first for the people who will actually use it, with a map you draw on instead of forms you fill in.

Factors the team considered

Farmers first: crop rotation and choices based on weather,place and soil type, small plots, low literacy in places, and patchy internet — so plain Bangla words along with English, pictures over text, and SMS alerts planned for weak-signal areas.

Honesty: no yield or income promises; every scenario figure is labelled "to be verified locally" with the rover data and expert suggestions from the agricultural officer to take the right choice for crop rotation and increase soil strength.

Cost: free NASA data and a cheap rover, so the system can start without expensive hardware. Local knowledge: officers who know the land review every case. And dignity: the farmer is smart and experienced — they need better clues, not pity or instructions from above.
